newsitem.title: MEXICO: Bell Atlantic deal to ease Iusacell scandal.
newsitem.headline: Bell Atlantic deal to ease Iusacell scandal.

text.p: By Henry Tricks,

The agreement by Bell Atlantic to assume management control of Mexico's Grupo Iusacell will help dispel the taint of scandal that has dogged the Mexican cellular phone company this year, analysts said on Tuesday.

Often during 1996, one of the owners of Iusacell, industrialist Carlos Peralta, has hit the headlines, partly because of a controversial payment of $50 million he admits he made to the jailed brother, Raul, of former President Carlos Salinas.
His tax returns are also being audited by the Finance Ministry, his spokeswoman Teresa Bermea told Reuters, which analysts say may also have made Bell Atlantic uncomfortable.

Rizwan Ali, telecommunications analyst at Bear Stearns in New York, said the controversy may have held up the granting of a fixed wireless telefony concession by the government, and persuaded Bell Atlantic to distance Iusacell from Peralta.
Bell Atlantic owns 42 percent of Iusacell. The other 48 percent is in the hands of the Peralta family, through parent company Grupo Iusa.

A top Mexican official has privately made it "very clear that the whole issue of allegations against the Peralta family has set back the timetable of granting a (fixed wireless) license to Iusacell," Ali said.
Another Mexican telephone analyst, who asked not to be identified, said that may be one of several reasons why Bell Atlantic pushed to take over management of the firm.

"They have not been happy in general with Peralta," he said. "Clearly they don't feel comfortable with someone under scrutiny by the authorities and they've had the Finance Ministry scrutinizing his books day in and day out."

On Tuesday, Bell Atlantic and Grupo Iusa announced that the U.S. telephone giant would assume management control of its Mexican partner, swapping B and D shares for some of the Peralta family's A shares, and paying a $50 million premium.

Bell Atlantic will also issue Iusacell $150 million in subordinated debentures, convertible into series A shares at $7 per ADS. A top Iusacell finance official, who asked not to be identified, said if they are converted it would lead to a new issue of A shares. The timeframe was not clear.
If he wishes, Peralta can also withdraw entirely from Iusacell, selling his full stake in the firm in three chunks over three years.
But analysts said the deal may fall foul of Mexico's foreign investment law, that limits foreign voting control in the telecommunications industry to 49 percent.
Bell Atlantic said earlier today the share swap would not affect the aggregate share ownership of the company.

However, the $150 million debentures convertible to series A shares might push Bell Atlantic over the limit and a possible sale by Peralta certainly would. The company's series A shares are closely held by the Peralta family and not publicly quoted. A Iusacell official said earlier today she did not know the value of the A shares off hand.

"The final accord is subject to the authorization of the necessary (government) ministries," the Iusacell official said, acknowledging the investment law was a problem. "Everything depends on government approval."

If it goes through, analysts said it would be good for Iusacell, providing it with Bell Atlantic's capital and know-how to enable it to make further inroads into Mexico's cellular and fixed wireless local market.

Martin Lara, analyst at Caspian Securities, estimated the company would need to invest some $500 million to $1 billion in fixed wireless systems before the end of the century if it wins the long-awaited concession.
It also removed doubts about Bell Atlantic's commitment to Iusacell, that have clouded the long-term horizon.
"There is a commitment (by Bell Atlantic) to be in the market with Iusacell, which at some point not far back there was a question mark about," Bear Stearns' Ali said.
